summary: This informational RFC describes ECCSI, an elliptic-curve digital signature scheme for identity-based cryptography. It is certificateless, so no certificates are needed to authenticate identity, and it aims for low bandwidth and low computation. It is not a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Ordinary digital signatures need a certificate, a document from a third party that says whose public key this is. That document costs bandwidth and storage. ECCSI removes it: the key is tied to the signer's identity string by a central key management service, and the receiver can check a signature knowing only that service's public key and the signer's identity.

subtitle: A digital signature scheme where the public key comes from the signer's identity string, so no certificate is needed.

tldr.problem: Ordinary digital signatures need a certificate, a document from a third party saying whose public key this is. In low-bandwidth or resource-constrained environments that certificate is costly to transmit and store.
tldr.mechanism: ECCSI derives the signer's public key from the signer's Identifier and a root key held by a Key Management Service, which binds a secret signing key to that Identifier with a Public Validation Token. The signature is the same shape as an ECDSA signature, with the token appended.
tldr.outcome: Authentication happens in one transmission with no per-session reference to a third party, and the receiver needs only the KMS public key and the signer's identity string.

today: RFC 6507 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. It is a published algorithm rather than a Standards Track specification, and it is written to be used with the identity-based encryption scheme in RFC 6508.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Digital signatures provide authentication services across a wide range of applications, and a chain of trust for such signatures is usually provided by certificates. In low-bandwidth or other resource-constrained environments, the use of certificates might be undesirable. This document describes ECCSI, an efficient scheme for elliptic curve-based certificateless signatures, primarily intended for use with Identity-Based Encryption schemes such as the one in RFC 6508. As certificates are not needed, the need to transmit or store them to authenticate each communication is obviated. The algorithm draws on ideas set out by Arazi and is originally based upon the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, one of the most commonly used signature algorithms.

The algorithm is for use where there are two parties, a Signer and a Verifier; where short unambiguous Identifier strings are naturally associated with each of these parties; where a message is to be signed and then verified, for example to authenticate the initiating party during an identity-based key establishment; and where a common Key Management Service (KMS) provides a root of trust for both parties. The scheme does not rely on any web of trust between users.

Authentication is provided in a single simplex transmission without per-session reference to any third party, so the scheme suits situations where the receiving party need not be active, or even enrolled, when the message is sent, or where the number of transmissions is to be minimized for efficiency. Instead of having a certificate, the Signer has an Identifier to which the Secret Signing Key (SSK) has been cryptographically bound by the KMS by means of a Public Validation Token (PVT). Unlike a traditional public key, this PVT requires no further explicit certification. The verification primitive can be implemented using a projective representation of elliptic curve points, without arithmetic field divisions, and without explicitly using the size of the underlying cryptographic group.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary digital signatures need a certificate, a document from a third party that says whose public key this is. That document costs bandwidth and storage. ECCSI removes it: the key is tied to the signer's identity string by a central key management service, and the receiver can check a signature knowing only that service's public key and the signer's identity.

sections.title: Architecture and Key Material
sections.content:
A KMS provisions key material for a set of communicating devices, a user community. Each device must have an Identifier (ID), which can be formed by its peers. Identifiers must be unique to devices or users and may change over time, so all applications of the scheme must define an unambiguous format for Identifiers.

In advance, the KMS chooses its KMS Secret Authentication Key (KSAK), the root of trust for all other key material in the scheme. From this the KMS derives the KMS Public Authentication Key (KPAK), which all devices require in order to verify signatures, and this is the root of trust for verification. Before any signature is verified, members of the user community are supplied with the KPAK; the supply must be authenticated by the KMS and that authentication must be verified by each member of the user community. Confidentiality protection may also be applied. The algorithms assume one KMS, one user community and hence one KPAK, though applications may support multiple KPAKs, some of which could be private to certain communities; the method for determining which KPAK to use when more than one is available is out of scope.

The KMS generates and provisions key material for each device. It must supply an SSK along with a PVT to all devices that are to send signed messages, and the mechanism by which those SSKs are provided must be secure, because the security of the authentication ECCSI provides is no stronger than the security of this supply channel. Before using the supplied key material to form signatures, the Sender must verify the SSK against the root of trust, the KPAK, and against its own ID and its PVT.

During the signing process, once the Signer has formed its message it signs the message using its SSK. It transmits the Signature, including the PVT, and may also transmit the message where the message is not known to the Verifier. The Verifier then uses the message, the Signature and the Sender ID in verification against the KPAK. The SSK is an integer and the PVT is an elliptic curve point. The SSK must be kept secret, to the Signer and the KMS, but the PVT need not be kept secret. A different SSK and PVT pair is needed for each Signer ID, and the KMS may create multiple pairs for the same Identifier if necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one central service, the KMS, and two kinds of key. The KPAK is its public half and the trust anchor everyone checks against. Each device gets a private signing key and a public validation token from the KMS, tied to the device's identity string, and the device checks that pair before it trusts it.

sections.title: Parameters and Representations
sections.content:
ECCSI relies on elliptic curve arithmetic. The curve is defined by the equation y^2 = x^3 - 3*x + B modulo p, where B is an element of the finite field F_p of p elements, p prime. Points other than the group identity are represented as P = (Px,Py), with the affine coordinates satisfying Py^2 - Px^3 + 3*Px - B = 0 modulo p.

Canonical representations matter, because they are what makes implementations interoperate. Integers must be represented as an octet string with a bit length that is a multiple of 8, most significant bit first and padded with zero bits on the left, and when transmitted or hashed such octet strings must have length N = Ceiling(lg(p)/8). Elements of F_p must be represented as integers in the range 0 to p-1 using that representation, also with length N. Elliptic curve points must be represented in uncompressed form as 0x04 || x' || y', where x' and y' are the N-octet strings representing the coordinates.

The static parameters are fixed for each implementation and must be specified for each user community, though they may be shared across multiple KMSs. They are: n, the security parameter and the size in bits of the prime p; N = Ceiling(n/8), the number of octets used to represent the fields r and s in a Signature and also the number of octets output by the hash function; p, a prime number of size n bits; E, an elliptic curve over F_p with a subgroup of prime order q; B, the element of F_p that defines the curve; G, a point on E that generates the subgroup of order q; q, the order of G in E over F_p; Hash, a cryptographic hash function mapping arbitrary strings to strings of N octets; and the method for deriving user Identifiers, whose format must be specified by each implementation and which must be derivable by each device for every device it needs to communicate with. It is recommended that p, E and G are chosen to be standardized values, in particular the curves and base points defined in FIPS 186-3.

The community parameter is the KPAK, which must be supplied to devices each time the root of trust changes. It must be provisioned in a trusted fashion, so that each device has assurance that it is the genuine KPAK belonging to its KMS, and before use each device must check that the supplied KPAK lies on the elliptic curve E. The KMS must fix the KPAK to KPAK = [KSAK]G, where the KSAK must be chosen to be a random secret non-zero integer modulo q and must be kept secret to the KMS.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC fixes the exact byte layout of every value so that two implementations agree on the same numbers. It also fixes the curve parameters that a user community must agree on, and says the curve and base point should be the standardized ones from FIPS 186-3.

sections.title: Algorithms: Signing and Verification
sections.content:
Creating the key pair. The KMS constructs an SSK and PVT pair from the Signer's ID, the KMS secret and the root of trust. It chooses v, a random ephemeral non-zero element of F_q; computes PVT = [v]G in canonical form; computes the hash HS = hash(G || KPAK || ID || PVT) as an N-octet integer; computes SSK = (KSAK + HS * v) modulo q; and, if either the SSK or HS is zero modulo q, erases the SSK and aborts or restarts the procedure with a fresh value of v. It then outputs the pair and erases v. The method for transporting the SSK to the legitimate Signer device is out of scope, but the SSK must be provisioned in a way that protects its confidentiality.

Validating a received SSK. Every SSK must be validated before being installed as a signing key. The Signer validates that the PVT lies on the elliptic curve E; computes HS = hash(G || KPAK || ID || PVT), an N-octet integer that should be stored with the SSK for later use; and validates that KPAK = [SSK]G - [HS]PVT.

Signing. To sign a message M the Signer needs the KPAK, its own Identifier ID, its SSK and its PVT. It chooses a random ephemeral non-zero value j in F_q; computes J = [j]G in canonical form and assigns to r the N-octet integer representing the x coordinate of J; recalls or recomputes HS and computes HE = hash(HS || r || M); verifies that HE + r * SSK is non-zero modulo q and, if the check fails, aborts or restarts with a fresh value of j; computes s' = (((HE + r * SSK)^-1) * j) modulo q and then erases j; and sets s to q - s' if s' is too big to fit within an N-octet integer, or to s' otherwise. The RFC explains why that last step is needed: because p is less than 2^n, Hasse's theorem on elliptic curves gives q < 2^n + 2^(n/2 + 1) + 1, so if s' is greater than 2^n then q - s' is small enough and s is guaranteed to fit within an N-octet integer. The output is the Signature, that is r || s || PVT.

Verifying. To verify a Signature against a Signer's Identifier, a message and a pre-installed root of trust, the Verifier must check that the PVT lies on the curve E; compute HS = hash(G || KPAK || ID || PVT); compute HE = hash(HS || r || M); compute Y = [HS]PVT + KPAK; compute J = [s]([HE]G + [r]Y); and then check that the x coordinate of J equals r modulo p, and that it is non-zero, before accepting the signature as valid. The parameter q is not needed during verification. The ID, the message and the KPAK are anticipated to be implicitly understood because of context, but any of these values may also be included in signalling.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four steps. The KMS makes the key pair from the identity string. The device checks the pair it was given. The device signs by picking a random number and mixing it with the key and the message. The receiver recombines the same values and checks that the result matches the r the sender included.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The ECCSI cryptographic algorithm is based on ECDSA. In fact, step 5 of the verification algorithm is the same as the verification stage in ECDSA. The only difference between ECDSA and ECCSI is that in ECCSI the 'public key', Y, is derived from the Signer ID by the Verifier, whereas in ECDSA the public key is fixed. It is therefore assumed that the security of ECCSI depends entirely on the secrecy of the secret keys, and that recovering secret keys requires computationally intensive cryptanalytic attacks.

The KSAK provides the security for each device provisioned by the KMS and must not be revealed to any entity other than the KMS that holds it. Each user's SSK authenticates the user as being associated with the ID to which the KMS assigned it, and must not be revealed to any entity other than the KMS and the authorized user. The order of the base point G used in ECCSI must be a large prime q; if k bits of symmetric security are needed, Ceiling(lg(q)) must be at least 2*k. It is recommended that the curves and base points defined in FIPS 186-3 be used, but if other curves are used, the security of the curves must be assessed. To ensure that the SSK is only received by an authorized device, it must be provided through a secure channel, and the strength of the authentication the scheme offers is no greater than the security provided by that delivery channel.

Identifiers must be defined unambiguously by each application, and it is not necessary to use a hash function to compose an Identifier string, so weaknesses caused by collisions in hash functions can be avoided without reliance on the structure of the Identifier format. Applications may include a time and date component in their Identifier format, to ensure that Identifiers, and hence SSKs, are only valid for a fixed period of time. The use of the ephemeral value r in the hash HE significantly reduces the scope for offline attacks, and if Identifiers are specified to contain date-stamps then identifiers, SSKs, signatures and hash values periodically become deprecated automatically, reducing the need for revocation and other management methods. The randomness of the values stipulated to be selected at random is essential to the security provided: if the KSAK can be predicted, any signature can be forged; if the value of v used by the KMS can be predicted, the KSAK could be recovered; and if the value of j used by a user is predictable, that user's SSK could be recovered. In most instances the value s in the signature can be replaced by q - s, so the malleability of ECCSI signatures is similar to that in ECDSA: available, but also very limited.
sections.plainLanguage: The security rests on three secrets staying secret: the KMS master key, each device's signing key, and the random numbers picked along the way. If any of them can be guessed, signatures can be forged. Putting a timestamp in the identity string gives keys an expiry date, which reduces how much revocation machinery is needed.

items.title: Construct the key pair
items.text: The KMS picks a random v, computes PVT = [v]G and SSK = (KSAK + HS * v) modulo q.

items.title: Validate the SSK
items.text: The Signer checks the PVT is on the curve and that KPAK = [SSK]G - [HS]PVT.

items.title: Sign
items.text: The Signer picks a random j and outputs r, s and the PVT as the signature.

items.title: Verify
items.text: The Verifier recomputes HS and HE, forms Y and J, and checks the x coordinate of J against r.
